title: Low-cost, reliable insurance for previously uninsurable livelihoods

concept.text: The proposed innovation is affordable contractual protection for people whose livelihoods existing insurance serves poorly: cover that is understandable, inexpensive to administer and dependable when an insured shock causes actual harm. The objective combines access with reliability. Selling a low-premium policy would be insufficient if its payout rules routinely missed serious losses, its exclusions were poorly understood or its provider could not meet its obligations.

Smallholder agriculture illustrates the problem. The supplied World Bank summary describes how serving rural and remote communities, assessing losses in the field and obtaining information about farming practices can make traditional insurance prohibitively expensive. Index insurance reduces some assessment burdens by tying payments to an observable indicator, such as rainfall. Its central tradeoff is basis risk: the payment determined by that indicator can differ from an individual farmer’s actual loss. Extending reliable protection beyond smallholder agriculture to other irregular livelihoods and multiple perils is part of the proposed innovation, rather than an achievement established by this evidence.

significance.text: If affordable policies reliably responded to covered harm, they would extend usable contractual risk protection to livelihoods that currently lack it or receive unreliable protection. The direct advance would be a dependable claim on financial support after an insured shock. Its revolutionary importance would depend on how many underserved people it reached, how consistently it protected them and whether the arrangement remained financially sustainable. The supplied source grounds this access problem for smallholder farmers; it does not establish comparable results across livelihoods.

Better protection could make households and businesses more willing to invest, and could improve their ability to withstand shocks without lasting losses of productive capacity. These are conditional downstream possibilities requiring separate evaluation. The World Bank summary reports heterogeneous investment effects, so expanding insurance access cannot be assumed to produce uniform investment gains or poverty reduction.

Conceptual limit: cheaper measurement is only one component of affordable insurance. Better observation can help determine when payments are due, but it does not itself supply the funds needed to pay claims. Likewise, contractual cover protects against specified events and losses; it cannot be equated with a guarantee of income or protection against every source of hardship. These are design distinctions, not findings demonstrated by the supplied study summary.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a workable combination of low delivery costs, adequate information and reliable correspondence between covered losses and payments. The documented engineering and institutional barriers include expensive field verification, limited insurer knowledge of farming practices and basis risk. A system must reduce the expense of observing losses without losing the information needed to identify people who have actually suffered covered harm.

Design synthesis: remote sensing, digital verification and improved agricultural measurement could contribute to this capability, but the central advance would remain insurance design and risk financing. An accurate regional indicator is not automatically an accurate measure of every policyholder’s loss. The unresolved task is to connect measurements, contract terms and payment decisions closely enough to protect individuals while retaining the cost advantages needed to serve small policies. The supplied review does not establish that any particular technology has solved this combination of requirements.

Additional proposed requirements concern private information, claims manipulation and the financing of correlated disasters. Verification procedures would need to remain dependable under strategic behavior, while capital, reinsurance or explicit public support would need to cover obligations when many insured people suffer losses together. As a conceptual financing distinction, reducing measurement costs does not diversify a shared disaster loss. The supplied source does not establish the extent of manipulation, evaluate solutions to it or substantiate a particular correlated-risk financing arrangement; those parts of the original problem remain requirements to investigate.

current_state.text: A World Bank article by Pauline Castaing and Jules Gazeaud, published July 8, 2025, reports that index insurance can lower some administration and loss-assessment costs. Its account also describes uneven uptake and the possibility that index-triggered payments fail to match actual losses. These are relevant advances and limitations within smallholder insurance, rather than evidence that broadly applicable, reliable livelihood protection has been achieved.

The article summarizes evidence pooled from eight experiments in Africa and South Asia and reports substantial variation in measured investment effects. This gives the proposed innovation an empirical starting point: insurance can affect investment, but effects differ across settings, and extrapolation to new populations remains uncertain. The supplied record does not provide numerical effect sizes that can responsibly be carried into this record, nor does it establish poverty reduction or successful coverage across multiple livelihood types and perils.

The evidence available here is an accessible author summary of research, not a full independent audit of insurance products. The supplied review reports that the blog’s identity and complete extracted text were verified, with no reported truncation or extraction problems. It relied on the narrative without inspecting Figure 1, and the underlying journal paper was not supplied. Accordingly, the eight-experiment finding is presented as the blog’s account. Although the source index records retrieval on November 11, 2026, that retrieval does not establish research currency: developments through November 1, 2026 remain unverified in the supplied record.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: offer understandable, affordable insurance to diverse underserved populations, covering several clearly specified perils over multiple years. Report the populations, livelihoods, locations, contract terms and observed shocks actually included. Such a demonstration would establish breadth within those tested conditions; finite trials could not establish literal universality or reliability under every future disaster.
completion_criteria.label: Understandable, affordable multi-peril insurance serves diverse underserved populations over years

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reliability and financing assessment: independently compare payments with verified covered losses, including cases where losses occurred without a payment and payments occurred without corresponding losses. Audit exclusions, payment timing, disputes, appeals and insurer solvency. Account for the full costs of administration, verification, distribution, capital, reinsurance and subsidy, so that apparent affordability is interpretable. Any judgment of commercial or public financial sustainability should state which continuing support it assumes.
completion_criteria.label: Independent audits assess payment reliability, solvency and full insurance costs

completion_criteria.text: Proposed outcome and reproducibility assessment: use credible evaluations to measure financial resilience, investment responses and unintended incentives, alongside uptake, retention and understanding of the contract. Make methods, outcome definitions and sufficiently protected evidence available for independent assessment, and seek replication across materially different settings. These are proposed evaluation requirements, not established standards or a protocol prescribed by the supplied source. They respond to its documented heterogeneity and call for more evidence on cost-effective smallholder risk management at scale.
completion_criteria.label: Credible outcome evaluations enable independent assessment and cross-setting replication

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: FIN-05, “Scalable financing for creditworthy people and firms without conventional credit histories,” shares the challenge of serving people with limited conventional information and small or irregular financial needs. Its central problem is extending credit and assessing repayment prospects; FIN-04 concerns contractual compensation for covered losses. FIN-06, “Universally accessible, near-instant cross-border money transfer,” could help deliver premiums or payouts, but efficient transfers do not establish suitable coverage or dependable claims funding.

Roster-based synthesis: FIN-02, “Causal forecasting and prevention of systemic financial cascades,” and FIN-08, “A causal theory linking trading activity to market-wide liquidity crashes,” concern mechanisms through which financial losses spread or market liquidity deteriorates. Their connection to FIN-04 is the possibility of shared shocks and stress on financial providers. Livelihood insurance must meet its own contractual obligations during such stress; it does not by itself explain or prevent systemic cascades or trading-driven liquidity crashes.

Roster-based synthesis: FIN-03, “Run-resistant financing of long-lived, illiquid investment,” overlaps through the need for financing arrangements that remain dependable under stress. Its defining challenge is maintaining funding for illiquid investment, whereas FIN-04 must finance uncertain insured claims. FIN-01, “A general, testable theory of asset prices under adaptive behavior,” could be relevant to valuing risk-bearing assets and liabilities, but a theory of asset prices would not by itself solve loss verification, basis risk or insurance delivery costs.

Roster-based synthesis: FIN-09, “Causal measurement of investment’s financial and real-world impact,” connects directly to evaluating whether insurance changes investment behavior or improves resilience. FIN-04 is a proposed protective service; FIN-09 concerns identifying the effects of investment. FIN-11, “Operational limits on the financial value of information and arbitrage,” shares questions about the value and limits of better information. More precise loss information may improve insurance decisions, while leaving unresolved how much protection is affordable and who bears the losses.

Roster-based synthesis: FIN-07, “Cash-like privacy and resilience for digital money,” could inform the privacy and reliability of digital insurance payments, while remaining distinct from the policy’s coverage and solvency. FIN-10, “Scalable financing mechanisms for pure public goods,” may connect where shared measurement infrastructure or public support is involved. Individual insurance contracts do not automatically constitute pure public goods, and any subsidy or shared infrastructure would need to be evaluated separately from the performance of the insurance itself.

unresolved_issues: The underlying journal paper and Figure 1 were not inspected in the supplied review; numerical effect sizes, experiment-level methods and the full strength of the pooled findings remain unassessed here.
The supplied record does not establish developments through November 1, 2026; the November 11, 2026 retrieval timestamp does not resolve that gap.
Evidence for extending the capability beyond smallholder agriculture in Africa and South Asia to other livelihoods and multiple perils remains absent from the supplied materials.
The extent of claims manipulation and the effectiveness and cost of countermeasures remain unestablished by the supplied source.
The source does not substantiate a particular approach to financing correlated disasters or quantify the capital, reinsurance or subsidy needed.

Acceptable premiums, payout delays, loss-payment mismatch, exclusions and solvency margins require explicit context-dependent targets; no numerical acceptance thresholds are established in the supplied record.
Whether broadly reliable insurance would produce sustained resilience gains, increased investment or poverty reduction remains an empirical question.

brief.title: Affordable insurance that protects people's livelihoods
possible: People whose work is poorly served by insurance could buy protection they understand and afford. When a covered disaster damages their livelihood, they could depend on a payment that matches the harm, backed by a provider able to pay.
why: For households and small businesses, dependable financial support after a shock could help preserve their ability to earn a living. It could also give them more confidence to invest in their work.

sources.showed: Their pooled analysis found that index insurance, which pays according to measures such as rainfall rather than individual losses, generally increased agricultural investment. Effects varied widely across settings.
sources.quote: The impact of index insurance differs widely across studies, and adjusting for basic household characteristics does little to explain this difference.
sources.cited_for: Insurance can encourage investment, but its effects depend strongly on the setting.
sources.not_established: The analysis does not establish dependable, affordable protection across different livelihoods and hazards.

sources.showed: In a trial in Mozambique and Tanzania, farmers offered drought tolerant maize seeds alongside insurance recovered better after shocks. The working paper was not peer reviewed.
sources.quote:
Compared to farms in control  villages, where shocks have persistent effects that 
reduce future investment and productivity, those with access to both drought tolerant seeds and 
multi-peril index insurance show greater resilience and immediately bounce back from shocks.
sources.cited_for: Combining seeds and insurance can help farmers recover after shocks.
sources.not_established: The combined treatment does not establish that insurance alone provides reliable, affordable protection.

sources.showed: A long-running trial in India found no systematic effect of rainfall insurance on agricultural investment. Payments also failed to produce measurable gains in consumption or savings.
sources.quote:
We find no systematic, long-term effect of insurance access or adoption on agricultural 
investment decisions.
sources.cited_for: Selling insurance and making payments do not necessarily improve household outcomes.
sources.not_established: The trial does not establish a financially sustainable product that delivers lasting livelihood protection.

sources.who: Matthieu Stigler, Apratim Dey, Andrew Hobbs and David Lobell
sources.showed: Using satellite yield data and simulations, this preprint showed that observing many fields over few years can make insurance appear more reliable than it is.
sources.quote:
We ﬁnd a substantive
downward bias leading to a systematic overestimation of insurance quality.
sources.cited_for: More detailed satellite data can still give misleading estimates of how closely payments match losses.
sources.not_established: The study identifies a measurement problem; it does not demonstrate a reliable insurance product.

sources.who: Jon Einar Flatnes and Michael R. Carter
sources.showed: A draft study used Tanzanian rice yield data to model satellite insurance with inspections farmers could request after missed losses. It estimated payments resembling those based on local harvests, at lower cost.
sources.quote:
Moreover, when combining this index with a possibility of an audit, this contract
closely mimics the payouts of an area yield contract, but at a fraction of the cost, as audits
are estimated to occur only 17% of the time.
sources.cited_for: Targeted inspections could improve payment reliability while limiting inspection costs.
sources.not_established: The modeled contract does not establish dependable payments or sustainable costs in routine operation.

shown: Trials have demonstrated parts of the goal. Boucher and colleagues found better recovery when farmers received access to drought tolerant seeds and insurance together. Castaing and Gazeaud found investment gains on average across eight experiments, but large differences between settings.

The central difficulty remains matching payments to actual harm cheaply. Flatnes and Carter modeled a way to combine satellite measurements with requested inspections. Stigler and colleagues showed how satellite data can also make payment reliability look better than it is.
missing: Affordable, understandable cover has yet to demonstrate reliable protection across diverse livelihoods and several hazards over years.
Payments must match covered losses without making verification too expensive or vulnerable to manipulation.
Providers need demonstrated funding to meet their promises when a disaster harms many customers together.
Lasting gains in households' ability to recover, invest and avoid poverty need convincing demonstrations across different settings.

milestones.label: Affordable, understandable insurance protects diverse livelihoods over years
milestones.explanation: A demonstration would have to cover diverse underserved populations against several specified hazards over years, with clear, affordable terms. This would establish breadth under the conditions tested.

milestones.label: Independent audits establish reliable payments and full costs
milestones.explanation: Independent audits would have to assess payments against verified losses, exclusions, delays, disputes, ability to pay and all costs, including subsidies. This would reveal whether protection is dependable and financially sustainable.

milestones.label: Credible evaluations withstand independent assessment and replication
milestones.explanation: Evaluations would have to measure recovery, investment, incentives, participation and understanding, with methods and protected data open to scrutiny. Replication in different settings would test whether benefits extend beyond a trial.

uncertain: Acceptable prices, payment delays, exclusions and gaps between losses and payments depend on the people and risks being covered.
The funding needed for shared disasters, and the cost of preventing manipulation, remain unresolved.
It remains uncertain whether broader protection would produce lasting gains in recovery, investment or poverty reduction.

page.title: Inclusive livelihood insurance
page.definition: Insurance for underserved livelihoods improves households’ protection against specified losses after premiums, with comprehensible contracts and providers able to pay. Index insurance pays from a measured indicator; basis risk is the mismatch between that payment and an individual’s loss.

goal.need: A survey of 294 insurers in 37 countries recorded 985 microinsurance products covering 344 million people in 2023, about 12% of an estimated market of almost 3 billion people. Climate-risk products reached 42 million people. These estimates include insurance beyond livelihood protection. Across eight agricultural index-insurance experiments, investment effects varied substantially; expanding coverage does not establish consistent benefits.

figures.caption: Microinsurance coverage reported in the 2024 Landscape study
rows: Covered by reported microinsurance products in 2023
figures.note: Climate coverage overlaps total coverage. These are survey estimates, not peer-reviewed estimates of effective livelihood protection.

statements.quote: 150 million poor and vulnerable people covered by microinsurance.
statements.context: The revised Vision 2025 sets this coverage target for climate and disaster risks; it is not a test of individual payout reliability.

statements.quote: The goal of inclusive insurance is to extend financial protection to those who would otherwise remain uninsured, helping them manage risks more effectively.

statements.body: Quality Index Insurance Certification, developed by UC Davis and RCMRD with USAID support
statements.quote: certifies that an index insurance product will at a minimum not leave a family worse off.
statements.context: QUIIC describes an agricultural index-insurance quality assessment using historical index and household data.

completion.title: Livelihood insurance delivers net protection in an independently replicated field evaluation.
completion.criterion: For a specified underserved population and insured peril, an independently repeated field evaluation confirms reduced consumption shortfalls or productive-asset losses after premiums, under its registered decision rule. The repeated deployment uses the same contract, price and declared subsidy arrangements, meets applicable solvency and claim-payment requirements, and verifies customers’ understanding of triggers and exclusions. Publicly subsidized insurance must also outperform an equal-cost cash-transfer comparison.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis of published minimum-value and consumer-protection criteria; no outside body located defines this combined completion test.
completion.basis: Searches of IAIS product oversight, ILO PACE, QUIIC/MQS, InsuResilience Vision 2025 and European Microfinance Award 2025 rules found component tests, but no joint completion threshold for price, loss protection, comprehension and financing. This test combines the minimum-value comparison with observed protection, regulatory compliance and replication. The 2026 Vision 2025 report describes impact and cost-effectiveness data as sparse and difficult to verify; the combined test remains unestablished by the cited results.

milestones.title: A livelihood insurance contract increases expected household welfare after premiums.
milestones.criterion: At the offered premium, expected household welfare, measured as probability-weighted utility, is greater with insurance than without it (insurance benefit > 0). Public support is compared with equal-cost cash transfers. For livestock, 24 candidate contracts back-tested over eight years in 15 Kenyan sublocations yielded 9–50% of perfect-index welfare benefits. A 2015 Tanzanian rice simulation estimated audits in 17 of 100 zone-years. These are model results; the Tanzanian draft and a 2022 preprint identifying downward bias in basis-risk estimates are not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: Feed the Future Innovation Lab for Assets and Market Access at UC Davis, Minimum Quality Standard, Brief 2018-04. This research criterion was developed for agricultural index insurance; its application to non-agricultural microenterprises is an extension.
milestones.threshold_quote: The purpose of insurance is to leave farmers better off than if they had no insurance at all.

milestones.title: A livelihood insurance product reaches customers in a regulator-supervised pilot.
milestones.criterion: The responsible supervisor permits a bounded pilot, and the livelihood insurance product is issued to customers within that authorization. IAIS describes limited sales for a limited period to test business sustainability; it prescribes no universal cohort size or duration. A 2014–2018 randomized study of 3,004 households in Mozambique and Tanzania demonstrates field delivery of insured seeds, but its report does not document regulatory sandbox approval.
milestones.set_by: International Association of Insurance Supervisors, Application Paper on Product Oversight in Inclusive Insurance, paragraph 135, approved on 23 November 2017. This is a recognized supervisory pathway, not a requirement that every jurisdiction use a sandbox.
milestones.threshold_quote: sell a limited number of products for a limited period to test the sustainability of the business.

milestones.title: A livelihood policy pays parametric claims within 10 working days, or 20 after a catastrophe.
milestones.criterion: A livelihood insurance product pays valid parametric claims within 10 working days after complete documents are submitted; for catastrophic events, the Philippine agricultural framework allows 20 working days after complete requirements. The clock starts with documentation, rather than the loss. The Mozambique seed-insurance study reports 43 kg of replacement seed paid to five households, but does not establish compliance with either deadline.
milestones.set_by: Philippine Insurance Commission, Agriculture Microinsurance Framework, Circular Letter 2015-53, paragraphs 39(f) and 41, dated 15 October 2015. These deadlines were published for agricultural microinsurance; they are comparison benchmarks, not Philippine legal requirements for unrelated microenterprise products elsewhere.
milestones.threshold_quote: claims shall be payable within ten (10) working days upon submission of complete documents.

milestones.title: A livelihood insurance field evaluation shows positive net protection after premiums.
milestones.criterion: A controlled field evaluation meets its registered success criterion for reducing post-shock consumption shortfalls or productive-asset losses at the premium actually charged, with declared subsidy and risk financing. The 2014–2018 Mozambique–Tanzania study (3,004 households) reports recovery for insured drought-tolerant seeds; the bundle does not isolate insurance. An eight-year Gujarat study (52 treatment and 48 control villages) found no systematic long-term investment effect or consumption/savings gains.
milestones.set_by: Atlas synthesis of the minimum-value objective and insurance impact evaluations. Searches of IAIS guidance, ILO PACE and QUIIC/MQS found no common field endpoint, minimum effect size or statistical decision threshold across livelihoods; the evaluation’s registered rule supplies those details.

not_found: No independently replicated evaluation meeting the combined completion test was located for non-agricultural microenterprise insurance.
No common numerical acceptance thresholds were located for household affordability, individual loss–payout mismatch or customer comprehension across livelihoods.
The supplied NBER revision and the underlying Journal of Development Economics article returned HTTP 403; accessible author summaries support the corresponding results here.
The full Landscape of Microinsurance 2024 PDF exceeded the web tool’s size limit; its publisher’s release supplies the survey figures.

results.finding: In a study with 2,974 baseline observations, insured drought-tolerant seed cost approximately 20% more.
results.detail: The study reports sales of the insured seed bundle, but does not document authorization by an insurance supervisor for a bounded pilot.
results.quote:
Seeds oﬀered for sale
in these villages came only bundled with the index insurance. The insurance, which was
not subsidized, raised the price of the seeds by approximately 20%.

results.finding: In a study with 2,974 baseline observations, access to insured drought-tolerant seed was associated with recovery after shocks.
results.detail: The evaluation reports resilience for the seed-and-insurance bundle, but does not establish that insurance independently reduced consumption shortfalls or productive-asset losses after premiums under a registered success criterion.
results.quote:
Compared to farms in control  villages, where shocks have persistent effects that 
reduce future investment and productivity, those with access to both drought tolerant seeds and 
multi-peril index insurance show greater resilience and immediately bounce back from shocks.

results.finding: In 52 treatment villages, rainfall insurance payouts were usually disbursed one or two months after the contract period ended.
results.detail: The report says policyholders did not need to file claims, but does not establish whether payouts met the specified deadline measured from complete documentation.
results.quote: Payout disbursal usually occurred one or two months after the end of the time period specified in the insurance contract.

results.finding: In a trial with 52 treatment and 48 control villages, insurance payouts did not translate into an impact on consumption or savings.
results.detail: The controlled evaluation reports no consumption or savings impact despite subsidies and premiums. The excerpt does not establish a registered success criterion for post-shock protection or declare the risk-financing arrangements.
results.quote:
Analyses of impacts on consumption and well-being proxies reveal that insurance 
payouts often act as a substitute for informal transfers; however, this does not translate 
into an impact on consumption or savings.

results.finding: Crop-yield simulations, with 500 runs per sample length, found up to 150% upward bias in a low index-quality measure.
results.detail: The bias can lead to underestimation of basis risk. The study does not evaluate a contract’s expected household utility at an offered premium.
results.quote:
This upward bias in theR2 is relatively large, and even larger in percentage terms, with an upward bias of 150% for low values of the quantile pseudoR2
measure.

results.finding: For 400 Tanzanian rice farmers, simulated willingness to pay for conditional-audit insurance was 12.5% above the actuarially fair premium.
results.detail: The expected-utility result assumes a risk-aversion coefficient of 1. The contract and premiums were simulated; the source does not establish welfare at an actual offered premium.
results.quote: In particular, for an individual with a CRRA of 1, the WTP for the area yield contract is 14% over the actuarially fair price, versus a 12.5% premium for the satellite based conditional audit contract.

results.finding: For 2,000 simulated Kenyan pastoralist households, at least half gained expected welfare from livestock index insurance at actuarially fair premiums.
results.detail: The model used a 10% strike contract and measured expected welfare through certainty-equivalent herd growth. Outcomes varied across households; some did not benefit.
results.quote:
At least half the households 
benefit from an IBLI contract with a 10% strike (slightly lower proportions for other strike 
levels) with the positive risk premium growth rates associated with the contract ranging up 
to almost 100%.

results.finding: Mongolia's index-based livestock insurance pilot sold policies to 2,410 herders in 2006.
results.detail: The report describes a geographically and temporally bounded pilot and says FRC participated in agent certification, but it does not document supervisor authorization of the pilot or its sales.
results.quote:
From the start of IBLI second Sales season in 1st of April 2006 and till to the end 10th of July 
2006, totally 2410 herders bought IBLI (BIP and DRP) and premium amount reached 86.0 million  
MNT.

results.finding: TrigaCash enrolled 66 policyholders, including customers with small market livelihoods, in the CBSI sandbox pilot.
results.detail: CBSI reports that the product was implemented under its regulatory sandbox and that the pilot continues to be monitored. A market vendor describes receiving support, but the number of microenterprise customers is not specified.
results.quote: Since customer onboarding began in November 2025, enrolment has reached 66 policyholders, including 39 women.

results.finding: ACRE Africa’s Kenyan insurance pilot, sample size not stated, reported payouts in 24 hours.
results.detail: The pilot included weather-index and picture-based insurance. The report does not state when the payout clock started or establish that it ran from submission of complete documents.
results.quote:
In the pilot, with the integration of  smart contracts into weather index and picture based insurance, 
payout timelines were drastically reduced by 97% from an industry average of 45 days to 24 hours.

results.finding: TrigaCash paid 35 policyholders, including people with small market livelihoods, within two weeks of heavy rainfall.
results.detail: The timing is measured from the rainfall event, not from submission of complete documents. The source does not give the number of microenterprise operators among the 35 recipients.
results.quote: All 35 policyholders received their payouts within just two weeks of the heavy rainfall event, demonstrating the speed and efficiency of parametric insurance in delivering timely financial support when it is needed most.

results.finding: Kenyan livestock insurance study, 673 households: 61 percentage point reduction in anticipated livestock sales.
results.detail: The outcome is intended rather than realized sales. Coupons offered 10–60% premium discounts, and estimates span a range of prices. The text does not establish a registered success criterion, net protection after premiums, or declared risk financing.
results.quote: The average impact results presented in Column (1) of Table 5 imply a large 61 percentage point reduction in the number of households who anticipated selling livestock in the short run in order to cope with the 2011 drought.

results.finding: Mongolian livestock insurance: among 642 herding households, insured households had 22–27% more livestock two years after the disaster.
results.detail: The study used matching rather than randomized assignment and did not report a registered success criterion or household premiums. Donors supported payouts after the disaster; positive protection net of premiums was not established.
results.quote:
Two years after
the disaster, insured households own between 22 percent and 27 percent more livestock, which is the key
indicator for welfare in rural Mongolia.
